stories.title: Ticket scalpers in S. Korea face fines of up to 50 times of resale price
stories.summary: South Korea enforces new anti-scalping laws imposing fines up to 50 times resale price and criminal penalties including prison for fraudulent ticket purchases and sales. Online platforms must verify buyers, report suspicious listings, and remove flagged tickets quickly; failure to comply can lead to fines. Whistleblowers receive rewards up to 50 million won or half the penalty; some ticket types like movie tickets are excluded, while esports tickets may be included under sports laws. South Korea’s Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism on Aug 28 began enforcing sweeping anti-scalping regulations that expose ticket resellers to administrative penalties of up to 50 times their total sales and introduce cash rewards for tipsters who report violations. The enforcement decrees, which are amendments to the Performance Act Enforcement Decree and the National Sports Promotion Act Enforcement Decree, took effect on Aug 28, six months after the parent statutes were revised in February. Under the previous law, only the resale of tickets originally purchased through macro programmes, which automatically and repeatedly input purchasing commands, was banned. The revised framework scraps that narrow definition. Resellers now face penalties whether or not macro software was used anywhere in the transaction, and buyers who circumvent or disrupt a seller’s fair-purchase process in order to resell tickets face the same exposure. The ministry described the two offences in the legislation as “fraudulent purchases” – bypassing an original seller’s fair-purchase process through technical means for the purpose of resale – and “fraudulent sale” – habitually or commercially reselling tickets above face value without the original seller’s consent. Both carry criminal penalties of up to one year in prison or a fine of up to 10 million won (S$9,807), plus confiscation of illicit gains. On top of criminal liability, the Culture Ministry may impose a separate administrative penalty — calculated at between two and 50 times the total sale amount – scaled to the number of tickets sold and the price obtained. Platforms and primary ticket sellers are also brought into the enforcement chain for the first time.

stories.title: ‘Confluence of errors’ led to Belgian tourist Celine Cremer’s death in Tasmanian wilderness, coroner finds
stories.summary: Coronor finds 31-year-old deviated from a walking track as dusk fell, four days before the winter solstice Overlapping errors, including a lack of preparation in near-freezing winter weather, contributed to the death of a Belgian tourist on a wilderness track. Celine Cremer set off on a walk at Philosopher Falls in Tasmania’s remote northwest on 17 June 2023, and was reported missing almost 10 days later. Continue reading...

stories.title: Identity of high-profile Queensland man drawn into extortion case to remain secret after court ruling
stories.summary: Man – referred to as MM by court – will keep his identity hidden after legal challenge against suppression dismissed The identity of a high-profile Queensland man drawn into a Cairns extortion case will remain secret, after the state’s supreme court threw out a legal challenge against a suppression order. The man – referred to as MM by the court – was drawn into an extortion case earlier this year . He is not a party to the case and is not accused of any offence. Continue reading...

stories.title: Former AFL star Nicky Winmar jailed for six months for assault on woman
stories.summary: Barrister for former St Kilda player says he will appeal both the sentence and the conviction for unprovoked assault in May 2025 Former AFL star Nicky Winmar has been jailed for six months for attacking a woman in a violent assault. Winmar, 60, dropped his head as he was sentenced in Bendigo magistrates court over the May 2025 assault against a woman at Cohuna in northern Victoria. Continue reading...
